subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my speech will be somewhat shortened by what has been said this afternoon by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka). I want to congratulate him and his compatriot in our group, the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny) upon their contributions to this house. They are a credit to themselves and an evidence of the real greatness of the Canadian people.
The 1947 budget was presented to us as one granting great relief to the income taxpayers of Canada. But reviewing the budget in its entirety and analysing its figures, I find that the greatest relief has not been in the income tax field at all but in the granting of exemptions from the excess profits tax as af December 31, 1947. It has been evident to the Canadian people and to us here for many, many months that monopoly enterprise as we know it in Canada has been putting pressure on this government to give it relief from the excess profits tax, along with its demands for the removal of price controls. Price controls were removed during the first few months of this year in spite of the tremendous increase in company profits which were being made in almost every field of Canadian industry. Attention has already been drawn to the tremendous increase that has taken place in company profits for 1946 in most of the industrial firms in Canada, and with the removal of price controls we shall find that these prices will rise abnormally. What justification the government had for removing price controls when profits were climbing as they were is best known to them. But the Canadian people are alert and are watching these things.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then the hon, member's prediction of gloom and despair is really a bogey. He actually expects prosperity?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I shall come to the point which the hon. member raises if he will listen.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You will be disappointed if we have prosperity.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The final surrender has been that this government, on top of taking price controls off, now permits the removal at the end of 1947 of the taxation of excess profits. It should be remembered that the excess profits tax was imposed as a check on profits arising out of war business. It will be remembered that this government passed a special order in council setting aside the legislation passed in 1939 which limited profits on war contracts to five per cent, when these industrial firms refused to make badly needed

The Budget-Mr. Castleden
war goods so long as that act remained in operation. The excess profits tax was a tax on above normal profits arising out of war conditions. We maintain that the present situation, under which these companies are still making excess profits, arises out of conditions which are a direct result of the war; namely, there is an abnormal purchasing power in the hands of Canadian people as a result of war savings, gratuities and so forth, and, in addition, the ordinary peacetime requirements of the Canadian people in food, clothing and other goods were not available to them during the war. There has been this long period of security of goods, linked with a long period of pre-war scarcity of purchasing power, so that today the demand for goods was never greater.
In view of those conditions the checks of price control should have been maintained. If they are to be removed the least we could expect was that the government would continue to tax excess or abnormal profits. But price ceilings are being removed and the companies can now charge on most commodities all that the traffic will bear. The scarcity of goods and the purchasing power in the hands of the people in the form of war savings and war gratuities provide an effective market, and for a few months the industrialists of this country will enjoy greater profits. They are going on a profit spree today. We are opening the floodgates to an inflationary period which, I fear, will bring its consequences, and unfortunately, while the industrialists and those who are making these profits are having their spree today, all the Canadian people will suffer and suffer deeply in what will happen afterwards. Higher prices mean higher costs of living, and higher costs of production. The agriculturalist is not able to keep up, and the falling wages mean lower standards of living. All the benefits of the prevention of inflation are going to be lost to the Canadian people.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member talks about falling wages. Would he give an example?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am talking about the natural fall in wages which will come as soon as the purchasing power of the Canadian people has been used up. With increased cost of living, savings will be taken away; people will not be able to purchase commodities at high prices and commodities will not be there.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is emotional
economics.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is one of the minister's balanced economies, speaking in a large w:ay. The Canadian people have been left to
the uncontrolled and unrestrained profiteering of those who control many of the necessities of life, and essential commodities, such as food, clothing and shelter. The government in power has finally yielded to the pressure put on by those who are engaged in the distribution of Canada's necessities at the expense of the great mass of the people. I maintain that the results will not be felt for a year or two, but they are inevitable. There will be first a greater concentration of wealth in the hands of a few; second, a rapid depletion of the purchasing power in the hands of the Canadian people-

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You hope.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -and a period of excess profits. When this is over and Canadians can no longer purchase, production will be reduced; wages will fall and lay-offs in industrial plants will then be common. To prevent these results, controls should be maintained, and, above all, excess profits should be taxed.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You want to see a depression.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I do not want to see a depression; I want to prevent it. The removing of controls and the allowing of an increase in profits, and then on top of that taking off the taxation on excess profits are two steps which make for an ultimate depression. The fight of the government of the country during the wrar to control inflation was an example to the world. The Canadian people benefited tremendously from the measure of control to which they subjected themselves, and they did so in most cases with very fine grace.
Great credit is due to the previous minister of finance for the way in which he dealt with those people, who came asking for special privileges and the right to increase prices. This saved the Canadian people from years of inflation. We were the envy of countries outside of Canada; we were looked upon as an example, but today that is gone.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We still are.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With prices going the way they are today, with costs soaring, with no limitation on them?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not so high.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hear hon. members to my right mumbling. They have complained that price control and rationing were killing the initiative of Canadian industrialists. Well, today they are really enjoying a very high profit era, according to all the financial reports
The Budget-Mr. Castleden

received today. The Canadian industrialist is now being given his freedom and initiative to clean up for himself. The government is apparently giving him a free rein. The present uncontrolled monopolistic enterprise system is dying throughout the world except in the United States and Canada. I doubt very much whether it could withstand another depression.
I now wish to compare the treatment which the government has given to these privileged industrialists by the removal of the excess profits tax, with the treatment which has been given to another group of people at the opposite end of the economic picture, people who seldom reach the income tax level. 1 want to place before the house the treatment that these people are receiving under the income tax regulations, and particularly in western Canada.
The farmers of Canada, like most Canadians, did not object to paying just and equitable taxes. That particular injustice with which I wish to deal has not affected all the farmers across Canada, because the present injustice arises out of particular government regulations and restrictions which were placed upon these farmers in western Canada during the years 1942 and 1943. In those years the wheat farmers and wheat growers were, by very necessity, singled out by special regulations by this government.
Back in 1945 the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented to the special senate committee on taxation a brief in which they protested against the inadequate and inequitable application of present income tax regulations to farmers, because those people who framed the present income tax regulations had apparently intended them for general business operations, and had failed to take into consideration the unique position in which the Canadian farmer found himself.
It is interesting to note that the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech intimated that the act was being revised. So far as the particular grievance which I wish to present is concerned, I fear that the revision will come too late. The damage has already been done and the injustice has been perpetrated; but I would urge the minister to have the act revised as quickly as possible. I would suggest also that in the name of what is proper, decent and right, steps should be taken immediately to right an injustice, which I am going to place before the house this afternoon. I think it is so glaring an injustice that it will arouse any fair-minded person who is familiar with its operation.
Two changes have been made in the farm income tax regulation, one which allowed the farmer who has a loss in any one year to charge that loss against the next year's operation. It was a rather useless piece of patchwork, because when a farmer gets into the position where he has an absolute loss in any one year, assessing him for income tax in the next year is not much of a relief.
The next amendment, which allowed the farmer to average his income over a period of five years, was the first real improvement, but it was apparently implemented by experts who were in touch with the situation, and it very nicely missed the most important year to the western grain farmer, namely, that of 1944. It has come too late to prevent grave injustice.
The complaint which I wish to present to the house-and I have mentioned it on several previous occasions-occurred in 1944. The Canadian people will remember that during 1942 and 1943, because of lack of shipping facilities and the war situation generally and the shortage of storage space and cars, the Canadian government found it necessary to place a quota against farmers delivering their grain. The government requested them, in an effort to assist in winning the war, to store their grain on the farm ready for the hungry people of the world and the armies in the field as soon as they could take it out. Again in 1943 a quota was placed against the farmer and he was requested to keep his grain on the farm. This the farmers did willingly. In some cases the quota was raised. It was as high as eleven bushels; but many of the farmers were compelled to take their production of those two years and store it on the farm at their own expense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Which was very profitable.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I shall show the hon. member in a moment how profitable it was. They did not even ask the government to pay them something on production for that year. In 1944 the farmer was asked to deliver his grain, since the starving people of the world and the armies needed it to help bring victory. In the spring of 1944 the farmers hauled in their grain as rapidly as possible, only to find in 1945 their patriotism rewarded by having all their surplus grain production which they had stored in 1942 and 1943, and delivered in 1944, raise them into the income tax group. The officials came along and took all that production and placed it in one year and charged against them all the moneys they had received in the one year. No appeal from the treatment of the taxation branch has been successful. Some years later the farmer, who never even suspected that he would be placed

The Budget-Mr. Castleden
in the income tax group, is called into town by the income tax inspectors and asked for the permit books. The books are checked and the income is assessed for that year. Let me give some examples of actual cases that came to my notice.
A. This farmer in 1942 had an income of $950. The grain was still on the farm. His expenses were $1,100. He had a loss of $150 in storing the grain on the farm.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How much grain
had he ?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There were several hundred bushels. In 1943 he had an income of $1,657 and his expenses amounted to 11,376, or a profit of $2S1. The grain is still on the farm, but he has not the cash income. Now we come to 1944. They ask him to deliver the grain and he hauls it out. In 1944 his total income was $4,764, and his expenses for that year amounted to $1,579, so that he had a profit of $3,185. On that he is taxed $380.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was that not spread over the three years?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, it was not, and that is the very point. In 1945 his income was $2,155 and his expenses were $1,237. He had a profit of $918.
This is the important point. His annual net profit over that period of four years was less than $1,100, or below the income tax level fixed by the Canadian people for a married man. '

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would it be plus his living?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: His living for himself and his family is chargeable. He has to mark that in his returns as so much produce taken from the farm.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why did he not show that he had so many bushels in stock? He should have shown that he had so many bushels.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He was not liable for income tax because these fellows never paid income tax. Even in 1945 he was not told by the income tax inspectors of that time that it was possible for him to go on the accrual basis. I will give the figures and the information he has to fill out, in order to indicate his difficulties. As I say, this man's annual income over that four-year period was some $1,100, which is less than the amount the government fixes as taxable minimum.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is not a fair
statement.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You are not taxed on any income less than $1,200 for a married man. This man was under the impression that he was doing a patriotic service by building granaries at his own expense and storing grain when the government could not take it. If he had been allowed to deliver his grain he would not have been taxable. He would have been in the same position as any other farmer in Canada. But because he is a western farmer growing grain trying to fulfil the regulations of the government he is forced into that position. He was not informed in 1944 of what would be done. He did not find out until 1945. Such people did not earn enough money in any year to make them liable for tax. Government regulations forced this man into tax levels by compelling him to withhold sale. He could not believe that he would be taxed for carrying out the government's instructions. He was willing to suffer a loss in 1942 of $150 and live on a miserable profit of $281 in 1943. His appeals to the taxation division in Regina were, however, unavailing. He was charged a five per cent penalty for late filing, and eight per cent interest was charged against his arrears for the period during which he had not paid. He received the following letter from the income tax division under date of March 5, 1946:
Re: 1944 income tax assessment-$416.67
It would appear that your income tax assessment is in arrears as noted above, notice of which was recently forwarded to you. Will you please make arrangements for settlement immediately as interest at the rate of 8 per cent per annum is accruing.
This is not an isolated case but one that can be repeated in every village, town and hamlet in my part of the country, where the income tax officials have suddenly swooped down on the district and called the farmers in.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is not only in the west.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I can give the figures for the east. Let me take now case B. This man in 1942 was not assessable; in 1943 he was not assessable; in 1944 his assessment was $298 and his tax was $56.
Let us take case C in the same town. In 1942 he was not assessable, nor was he assessable in 1943, but they got the permit books and checked deliveries in 1944 of grain grown and all the work done in 1942 and 1943. In 1944 he delivered 2,397 bushels of wheat, most of which was delivered during the months of January to June and therefore could not have been grown in 1944. This amount was taxed
The Budget-\lr. Castleden

$187.95 for that year on grain which he stored for the government and the people of Canada. As one farmer wrote to me:
They taxed me for two years' work and for storing my grain for them. I do not mind paying what is right but surely not this. If they think I will work and slave 16 to 18 hours a day and keep this grain for the government and then pay it over to the income tax, when they compel me to put all three years' production into the one year, they are badly mistaken. I will quit farming as soon as I can.
It is little wonder, then, that among the income taxpayers on the farm, the grain growers in western Canada, for the year 1945-46, Saskatchewan farmers paid more farm income tax than all the farmers of Ontario and Alberta put together, and that the grain growers of Manitoba were in many cases caught almost as badly.
If this is an example of justice as handed down by the present government it is little wonder that these fanners protest against it. The undeniable fact is that grave injustices were perpetrated under the present farm tax regulations. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech promised some action in the rewriting of the income tax act, which would indicate that he and his colleagues are aware that these wrongs and injustices exist.
The instances which I have given of injustices as applying to the grain farmers of the west are one explanation of the remarkable fact that in 1945-46 Saskatchewan farmers paid, for the 1944 income year, the sum of $2,587,632 in income tax, while Manitoba was caught similarly, whereas only 280 Quebec farmers were assessed and the total amount of their payments was $59,913.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Diversified farming.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, but they were allowed to deliver their produce. In this case, however, the government prohibited the farmers, by its regulations, from delivering their produce. What would your farmers say if there were regulations that prohibited them from delivering for a period of three years and then lumping it all in one and charging income tax on it? Yet that- is what is being done here, and in the whole of the maritime provinces only 318 farmers were assessed for income tax, their total payments amounting to $82,588.
I should like to review the kind of forms which the farmer has to fill out, Along with the regular information given in the special form, he has to give his income, gross wages, and net income from professional fees, net profit from farm or ranch, net income from rentals and income from interest, dividends and so on, and total income, subtracting donations to charitable organizations, medical [DOT]Mr. Castleden.]
expenses and so on. Then under section 13 there is a tax on item 12-K, found in the tax tables on pages 3 or 4, less a 4 per cent reduction of item A as per the 1945 statutes. Then there is C, tax after subtracting B from A, and
D,	less applicable portion, if any, of British and foreign income tax paid. Then there is
E,	tax after subtracting D from C, then there is the provision with regard to family allowance, under section 17, and so on.
What I am trying to point out is that the complicated income tax form is far beyond 'the comprehension and ability of an ordinary person to gather together the information and do all the arithmetical work and accounting necessary. On top of this, the farmers have to include the special T-l supplemental in which they give their farm receipts for the calendar year, showing their production from crops, grain; live stock, meats, et cetera; dairy products; fruits and vegetables; miscellaneous sales such as maple syrup and sugar; patronage dividends; produce raised on farm and consumed in the farm home. This is for garden produce, I suppose.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The government do not tax a person 'living anywhere else on that. I think it is absolutely ridiculous. Then farmers must show farm expenses; purchases of seed, purchases of live stock, cost of repairs and maintenance; general farm expenses; taxes on farm; interest paid; wages paid. The trouble is that very few farmers have the time to be accountants. What is required is a simplified form of farm accounting-

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Have you a sound proposition?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-where farmers can write down in a simple way what their produce is, what their income is for each member. The farmer is taxed as an individual for the income of the whole family. His wife and family all go together. The work of five or six is all lumped together and placed on the one man. That is not right. The form of the income tax forms put out by the government is unjust if you apply this type of thing to the average farmer.
The recent reduction in hog production in western Canada, which again this year shows a reduction, amounting to some thirty-seven per cent, can be traced to a large extent to the injustices which farmers feel with regard to their treatment under the farm income tax regulations.
Farm organizations have requested and suggested to this government, in view of the

The Budget-Mr. Castleden
peculiar nature of the set-up of farm industry, the violent fluctuations in income and the uncertainty of return for the work, that higher exemption be granted for every farmer for production in poultry, hogs and dairy products. If they would grant an exemption of $500 for the farmer in that type of thing, it would go a long way to relieve the feeling of injustice under which he is suffering.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The form would be more complicated.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think the form would be simplified, and it must be simplified. Exemption for farm income should be raised. There is not just the one man concerned. It is the man and his whole family. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture, in their 1947 annual convention, passed a resolution asking that the government increase the exemption to $2,400, if they are to maintain this type of return to be handed in by the farmer.
I realize that there are great difficulties in connection with this problem, by its very nature. The farmer does not keep records. If he had done so, and realized his actual position, I am afraid we should have had very few farmers left on the farms of western Canada to produce wheat. I think the same is pretty well true of farmers across the whole of the dominion. Those who have done that essential work need proper recognition, not discrimination and this kind of thing. I urgently request the government to implement immediately some change which will rectify this gross injustice which was done to the farmers in 1944.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that the matter of Canadian immigration is before a committee of this house and that one is not allowed to discuss the subject at this time. If I had the opportunity, I would voice a protest for the people of my constituency against the present regulations. I will, however, refer to what our sister dominion, Australia, has done. Although less favourably situated, she is doing a great job in providing the people of Australia with an immigration policy. I believe arrangements were made for that country to take in some fifty thousand orphans from Europe. The Canadian people know what Canada can do, and the excuse that we have not the shipping is just not good enough. The Australian government have undertaken a programme of converting their shipping into passenger boats to bring immigrants to that countiy, and their programme calls for some seventy thousand a year. Canada and this government achieved great things in the war. What we did in the way of the British empire air training plan,
our conversion in industry, in synthetic rubber production and the atomic bomb reveals what the Canadian people can do. The record is just too good for this government to turn around and say, "Oh, we can't do anything about it; we haven't the shipping." If the Canadian people and the Canadian government wanted the shipping, they could have it.
In closing, I should like to make a national plea for the government of this country and the Canadian people as a whole to realize what is happening and put a stop to what I will call the rapid Americanization of this Canada of ours. For years there has been a gradual draining off of Canada's wealth- our resources, human and material-to the great and wealthy nation to the south of us. United States capital is developing and controlling our natural resources such as pulp, minerals, oil and water power. Recent purchases, according to financial news, reveals the gradual passing of financial control of Canadian industry into the hands of United States capital. Wall Street is moving into Canada. During the war, control of a large block of Canada's water power was handed over to the subsidiary of a world aluminum combine. The Imperial Oil Company was granted by the federal government the sole right of exploration for oil and a large tract of oil-producing territory in the Mackenzie river basin. Holiinger interests have recently obtained the right to the development of what appears to be one of the greatest mineral resources in the northeastern part of Quebec and Labrador. Just a few days ago this house passed a bill to grant them the right and privilege of constructing a railway from the St. Lawrence river up into that area.
What is wrong with Canada? What prevents Canadian capital from developing Canada's resources for the benefit and welfare of the Canadian people? If Canada is to play her great part in interpreting the old world to the new and the new world to the old, we must make Canada here a land which will provide for our Canadian youth as a land of greatest opportunity for them, and a land which will attract the best from other countries. "Canada for the Canadians", might in many respects again become a slogan for the Canadian people if it is to prevent itself from becoming dependent upon a rich uncle to the south. We should be looking forward to the development of our own birthright, to making ourselves a growing nation, willing and capable of asserting herself as one of the united nations making her contribution to a world of peace.
The Budget-Mr. Picard

It would appear at the present time that some such spirit as this is necessary if we are not to be absorbed entirely by our rich and powerful neighbour to the south. We have been greatly enriched by the diversity of our population, each group making its own contribution through its wealth of culture and ability. It is now the duty of the Canadian people to show that their unity creates a strength which can illustrate to the world that the peoples of the world can work and unite, and by cooperating can make a contribution to a world of peace.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Picard

ant question of education. A country like ours needs more and more educated and well-informed citizens. The greatness of a country depends on the value of its citizens, and t'he service of the citizens to the community is influenced in no small degree by the extent of their knowledge. It is true that, under our present constitutional set-up, education is a provincial responsibility and prerogative, but this does in no way exempt the government of the country from contributing its share to the betterment of education in any way it can, or rather in any way in which the provinces will allow it to do so.
One of the best ways, it seems to me, would be to encourage parents to keep their children in school and college and, if gifted, send them to a university. We have seen by some figures given to us that the average income of wage-earners and of all gainfully occupied people is not so high as to enable all to enjoy a high standard of living, far less to enable many to divert a large part of their earnings to the higher education of their children.
There are two ways we could adopt to help remedy this situation. One would be to extend the age for family allowances in the case of children pursuing their studies past sixteen. That would be just a token of encouragement but it might help a little.
Another way would be to extend the special exemption of income tax to a higher age for children pursuing their studies. This, I know, has been advocated by others, but I have always felt so keenly about the charges that have to be borne by parents who understand the importance of giving their childen the best possible educational equipment with which to go through life that I feel I must join with other voices which have been raised in this matter.
There is another question I should like to mention in regard to the assessment of taxes on the farmers. I will admit that a very small number fall in the category of income tax payers, but in the case of those who do I have noticed an anomaly which may be peculiar to our part of the country but which at all events deserves our attention. Cases have happened of farmers who, when getting more prosperous, have been subject to income tax, and I think the assessment has been made without taking some most important elements into consideration. This has to do mainly with salaries to farmers' sons and other members of the family. Our Quebec farms are operated most of the time as a family concern. The children work on the farm from the moment they can and no salary above their bed and board is paid to them. They

contribute to the community and get no wages, but when they reach the age for marrying their father takes out of his accumulated capital, whether it is all in land or partly in cash, the value which he considers equal to his son's share in the prosperity of the family, and he gives him part of the land he has acquired during his life, or he gives him cash to buy a farm. This is a form of what I might call delayed salary. When the income tax assessors try to compute the actual income of that farmer over a number of years they do not accept that system and, in order to arrive at the income, they establish the capital and in it include the son's share as the father's gain. I think decent salaries should be allowed to farmers' sons in such income tax assessments. Whether they are paid monthly, yearly, or in a lump sum after a number of years should not be material. I commend this to the attention of the minister because I know personally of such cases and, this being a practice much followed in rural Quebec, it may be that others will have to suffer if the attitude of the department is not changed in this regard.
Now that I have advocated the reduction of taxes, I would not be following the regular pattern if I did not advocate some expenditures. I notice that it is a general practice on all sides of the house to complain about taxes and the next moment to put in a claim for public expenditures. I shall not impose on the house a list of the public works that would be needed in my constituency, but I should like nevertheless to submit to the government that consideration should be given at an early day to a programme of public works or capital expenditures in the country.
Wharves need to be rebuilt; public buildings are badly needed in many parts of the country; irrigation projects and other improvements are necessary. The time will quickly come, according to many economists, when men will again be looking for employment instead of jobs looking for men. The closing of war industries has been partly compensated for in some parts of the country by the reconversion to peacetime production, but in many parts of the country such readaptation has gone on more slowly and I cannot but feel that it is high time to start elaborate plans for a programme of public works, to be ready when the needs arise.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I may say that the budget now under consideration is a source of satisfaction and relief to a large part of the population. Owing to our actions of the past, it cannot be lightened much more, and we realize that the taxpayers of Canada are paying for what they wanted during the

The Budget-Mr. Bracken
war and for what they wanted in the way of social security for the period of peace. I think the cut in the sources of revenue is in the right direction, with the qualification I have made with regard to the excess profits tax.
Much has been said of our system of government in relation to others and of the necessity to fight for its preservation. I personally think it is better because it respects the individuals and their liberties, but let us not forget that our aim should not stop at respect for the freedom of the individual but should also include the improvement of his standard of living and his freedom from want. The time has come for the drafting of a far-reaching Liberal programme if we want our system to justify itself.
I believe it is right that the Liberal party in Canada should be the one to put it into effect. I believe that such a programme could easily be worked out under the system of improving the fate of the masses, while at the same time permitting a fair but reasonable return to those who, having worked and gained, are willing to risk their oftentimes hard-earned money in new commercial and industrial ventures.
Let us not get too panicky in our fears of communism. The best way to vindicate our present system is to work hard and plan well for the future. Some people consider our present form of capitalism as a permanent institution and fear the world will regress if it disappears. The same things were said when the French revolution gave a death-blow to monarchial systems throughout the world.
No system of government has yet proven itself perfect. I am quite satisfied that the present one with improvements is best suited for our country, but I am convinced that the world will experience many philosophies of government before it succeeds to give to all its inhabitants a fair and enjoyable life on this planet.
The government of the world has been in constant evolution and up to now it has never gone backwards for a very long period of time; its march has been onward. A proportionately larger number of people live well today than in the previous centuries, and I am confident that this will continue improving with the years and that Canada will rise to its opportunities and make for itself an ever larger place among the nations of the world.

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is not my expectation to speak at any length tonight. The debate has already continued for a considerable period and practically every aspect of the subjects dealt with has been referred to. Before the debate concludes, however, I wish to make some 83166-223i
observations on certain questions that are before the house and the country and then to state the position we propose to take with respect to the main motion and the two amendments made to it.
The motion by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is, in effect, a motion of approval of the government's budget. The amendment moved by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), and the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) are criticisms of that budget. It is these questions that we are now called to vote upon. I may say at the outset that when the subamendment comes up, which will be the first upon which a vote will be taken, we in this party will support these criticisms; and when the main amendment comes to be voted upon, we shall, of course, support it too. We shall support both of these amendments for the reason that the tax reductions are both inadequate and inequitable.
What are the issues upon which we are asked to vote tonight? I want to deal first with the main issues in the budget itself and then with the points raised by the two amendments. The government's tax proposals do two things: first, they perpetuate a tax burden 300 per cent greater than in any peacetime year. That is the main fact which we must not lose sight of in this debate. And they do one other thing. They reduce taxation by only seven per cent for this current year and by only twelve per cent for the year which follows. Those are basic facts in the government's budget position.
With respect to the amendments, they touch upon five points. They express regret that the budget provides no relief from indirect and hidden taxes; that the government offers no encouragement for the development of certain natural resources, such as agriculture and mining; that the government has failed to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference; that it has failed to raise the levels of income tax exemptions; and that it has failed to provide relief for the most needy half of the population of Canada. The question before us is, are these statements facts; are they correct, or are they not? To the extent that they are true the government deserves our censure.
I wish to ask first, is the statement of the government's fiscal position correct, namely, that the tax burden is 300 per cent greater than it wras in the highest taxation period prior to the war? And is it correct to say that there has been only a seven per cent reduction in this fiscal year and only a twelve per cent reduction for the next year in the present
The Budget-Mr. Bracken

budget? The facts are, from the government's own records, that the largest tax per year prior to the war was, in round figures, $550 million in 1939. The proposals in the present budget are in the neighbourhood of $2,200 million, or 'our times as much, or 300 per cent more than in that 1939 fiscal period.
The government's tax proposals this year, as I read the minister's address, are a reduction of S160 million this year and $265 million next vear, which, on the basis of the last year's budget, is a reduction of seven per cent for this year and twelve per cent for next year. We take the position that that degree of taxation is too high, and that those taxation reduction proposals are too little.
I want now to examine the statements of criticism as outlined in the two amendments, taking them in order, (a), (b), (c), (d) and (e). Does the budget provide relief from indirect and hidden taxes? The answer is no. No one in the house will dispute that answer. The reductions are confined almost wholly to the income tax. That part of the dominion's revenues collected from regressive taxes, the hidden and indirect taxes which bear heavily upon the poor, is not reduced in any way. That was the first criticism in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, a criticism which was expressed in different words in paragraph (e) of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar. As I said, regressive taxes are taxes which bear unduly upon the poor; and these taxes provide practically half of the revenues of the Canadian budget. There has been no reduction in those taxes. The consequence is that the poorest section of the nation receives no relief by this budget, even at a time when the cost of living is going up -it is said to have gone up three per cent in the last four months-and even at a time when the government has taken off subsidies amounting, in the total, to $200 million.
With respect to the second criticism in the main amendment, does this government offer any encouragement to the development of our natural resources, particularly the resources of agriculture and mining? We maintain they do not. The policies of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) have the whole country baffled. I wonder if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself knows what the Minister of Agriculture is up to. The Minister of Agriculture has the government handle all the wheat and sell it at prices that force the farmer into growing coarse grains; then the government seizes the coarse grains and
disposes of them in Canada at prices that encourage the production of bacon; then it finds that it cannot fill its bacon contracts with the old country and calls upon the taxpayers of Canada to put up, as some estimate, twenty-five per cent by way of bonus for every hog that Britain buys.
These are basic things in the government's agricultural policy. Our agricultural and mining policies are the two sections of our economy which should, if properly managed, help us with the solution of both our internal and external problems.
You may ask, how is the government failing the farming industry? It practically denies the farmer the dollar market in the United States. It practically shuts us out, and even outside the dollar market it makes the farmers sell at prices lower than those received by their competitors in the British market. It makes our contracts in Canadian dollars and then does nothing to protect the value and integrity of the Canadian dollar. It asks us to sell our products to Britain and other countries on time, at prices lower than other countries are demanding and getting. We are denied the market across the line where we could get higher prices and obtain United States dollars for which our economy is crying out so loudly.
In point of fact, the government's bilateral trade policies are imperilling our own exchange situation on this continent. It is selling huge amounts of our agricultural produce overseas at less than world prices and buying from the United States much more in the way of commodities than we sell to them. In the crop year 1949-50, all that the farmer is certain of is the Canadian dollar, and he has no idea what it will buy. In recent weeks the price of butter has increased ten cents, and 8^ cents of the increase is the withdrawn subsidy. The government gives with one hand and takes away with the other. There is no relief in the budget except for those who are reasonably well off. That is the basic criticism from the humane point of view.
With respect to mining, I will take only a moment to deal with that. It has been discussed fully by others. The government admits its own failure. Its action in revaluing the dollar on July 5 deprived Canadian gold producers of $3.50 for every ounce of gold sold to the United States. The government got panicky about holding the price line and our dollar situation has been going from bad to worse.
If these observations with respect to agriculture and mining are not accepted at their face value, I would refer to but one statement in a government document published

The Budget-Mr. Bracken
by the bureau of statistics. It is entitled "Canadian Constitutional Data". I will read only a portion of one paragraph. It has to do with the question of developing our own resources and whether we are doing enough in that direction. The statement is as follows:
Canada is one of the last countries to have her frontiers pushed back, and this process has not yet reached its limit, nor have the natural resources on much of the land been explored, exploited or harnessed.
This is from a government document published only within the last few weeks.
I come now to the third criticism in the main amendment. Has this government failed to reconvene the dominion-provincial conference? One has only to ask that question to answer it. A few months ago the government came forward with a programme in connection with dominion-provincial relations, and among other things it proposed a policy of social security, health insurance and public investment or public works-the purpose of which was partly to help head off depression. The combined policy was variously estimated to cost the different taxing jurisdictions in the country, S400 million or $500 million, or $600 million a year, when completed. This cost added to our present budget makes a total budget approximating ninety per cent of the highest wartime taxation we ever had.
What has happened? The government says, in effect, "We can only proceed with that policy if a large proportion"-it is a little vague about it-"of the provinces agree". Seven have agreed and two have not. The government now says it cannot proceed with that policy without having the assurance presumably of more provinces than have agreed, and yet the government does not call a conference. As a result, those policies which the government says are good, which it says it can only proceed with after some more general agreement, it now lets fall by the wayside because it fails to provide the opportunity for that more general agreement; and so those policies of social security and health insurance and public investment remain up in the air. Nothing is done. That is one of the criticisms in the amendment.
I come now to the first of the two criticisms in the subamendment. Has the government failed to raise the exemption levels in the income tax? Again one has only to ask the question to answer it. It has not. The question now is whether it should or should not have done so. The simple fact is that the government today is taxing people who are receiving less income than will maintain a decent
standard of living for many families in this country. If the government considers it is good policy to tax people who are already not getting enough income to pay their way, then the government's policy can be understood; but if it is bad policy to do that, then the government should be censured for its failure in this year's budget to give them relief.
The final criticism in the sub-amendment raises this question. Has the government failed to provide relief for the most needy half of the population? At page 2554 of Hansard the Minister of Finance said:
The exemption levels established last year are high enough to exempt completely from tax more than half the people earning incomes in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, on the statement of the minister half of the Canadian people have received no benefit from this budget-no relief whatever-at a time, as I said a moment ago, when their costs of living are going up and when this government has taken off the subsidies which formerly helped keep the costs of living down. If it is wise to give no relief to the most needy section of the Canadian population, then the policy of this budget is understandable. But if it is unwise to continue to ask the poor to bear an unfair share of the burden of taxation, then, as I said a moment ago, the government should be censured.
So much for the basic facts in the minister's motion and for the five criticisms outlined in the two amendments. I now wish to touch upon three or four other questions which have to do with us here and wdth our economy as well. The first is the question of foreign exchange control. Our United States dollar situation has been referred to several times in this debate. It was never so serious as it is now. As the hon. member for York South (Mr. Cockeram) pointed out, the report tabled in this house the day before the budget was brought down does not fully reveal the current situation. If the year that this report covers-1946-were divided into three-month periods our deficits and commodity trade with the United States would be shown as $93 million, $120 million, $126 million and $158 million-a steadily worsening situation. When it is stated in that manner, it means much more than when an average of those four figures is taken.
By contrast, we sold to Britain over S597 million worth of goods; and we were able to take from Britain, or Britain was able to supply to us only $201 million worth of goods. Yet Britain has taken up approximately
The Budget-Mr. Bracken

half of our one and a quarter billion dollar loan. On a per capita basis we are lending Britain more than four times as much as the United States did. We supported that policy, but what use will it be either to Britain or to ourselves if we assume a load which will crush us down? We may thus become more of a hindrance than a help to Britain. Last year we made her turn over to us $150 million worth of gold, three-quarters as much as she sent us in goods. It is clear from the minister's statement that the government has no present solution for the unbalanced United States dollar situation. All it can do is hope and pray that something will happen in the United States, though that something may be a recession which will do us harm.
This so-called dollar situation which, in other words, simply means the trade position, has always been a Canadian problem; as I said, it is particularly acute now. The facts behind it are these. On July 5 last our government became unduly apprehensive about United States prices and decided that they must do something to make it easier for Canadians to buy United States goods. The result is twofold. They have made it relatively too easy to buy from the United States, and relatively too difficult to sell to the United States. We maintain in Canada a price ceiling which they do not maintain in the United States. As long as we have this price ceiling there will be a gap between the amount of money coming to the counter and the amount of things on the counter. That surplus money for which there are not goods to spend it on in Canada drives purchasers to the United States to buy goods there. The remedy is one which has been referred to often in this house and elsewhere; it is increased Canadian production.
We have made bilateral deals which make it difficult for us to obtain United States dollars for our farm products. There are other considerations involved, I know. Nevertheless that is one of our great difficulties. Our present United States trade situation as it developed from July 5 is a perfect example of how controls work. One control makes another control necessary. The government decided to maintain a price ceiling, and therefore had to revalue our dollar so as to lessen the cost of United States imports. Now it finds adverse trade balances running against us more acutely month by month.
With respect to international trade generally, some of our policies are blocking, not promoting, the Geneva programme of multilateral trade and the lessening of restrictions against trade. The government talks multilateral agreements, but certain of its policies
cut across those of the whole international trade organization. We were given to understand that this government did not like the empire trade agreements. But now, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) says, the government regards the empire preferences as something quite precious. If the other countries at Geneva know as little about this government's trade policy as the government itself apparently knows, they surely must see through a glass dimly.
I now wish to refer briefly to one of the special commodities in connection with trade, and because it has been discussed so often and so fully in this house I shall be very brief. I refer to the subject of wheat. In my opinion, the British wheat agreement killed the London wheat conference, a conference which was called to try to get an international agreement with respect to wheat prices, wheat quotas and so on-a conference which failed. As I said, in my judgment the Canadian-British wheat agreement killed that conference. Why would Britain agree to a $1.80 price ceiling? She had already established a ceiling of $1.55 in the agreement made with this government a year or two ago. By contrast, her idea of a floor price was somewhere around $1; and that idea of a $1 floor price was also sold to Britain by Canada. Is it any wonder that Britain and some others objected when certain of the nations wanted a higher level than a $1 floor and a higher level than $1.55 as a maximum price? It was difficulties such as those which caused the break-down of that conference which had such great possibilities.
I now wish to add a word about the situation in Europe which, over many decades, has been the chief market for our surplus products. The United States is talking about facing the problem in realistic terms. They talk about getting back to lend-lease, as contrasted with loans. Mr. Acheson, then secretary of state, renewed pleas that congress provide $17 billion in post-war lend-lease. General Marshall has also spoken along similar lines. The United States is thinking in terms of big things, as we expect her to do. That must be done to reestablish Europe and restore a workable peace. But the United States is not tying one hand behind its back as it plans to undertake the job.
What are we doing? If it is good policy to help Great Britain or other parts of Europe by turning over our wheat at $1 less than the world price, it is the United States which should be doing it, and not us. But the reverse is the case. We cannot afford to continue to do it indefinitely. Yet we embargo the sale

The Budget-Mr. Bracken
of our farm products to the United States. If our farm products or a larger portion of them were sold to that country they would collect United States dollars, now so badly needed here, and they would, in addition, bring a larger measure of equity to our agricultural industry. As a matter of fact, if our farm products were allowed the benefit of world market prices, our United States dollar difficulty would be considerably lessened.
I come now to my final point, namely the menace of communism in Canada. The British and the United States governments are beginning to understand that a policy built on weakness, instability and appeasement, in dealing with Soviet Russia, is as futile, and as ineffective, as the same policy proved to be against the Hitler and Mussolini gangs.
Too many people have forgotten that it was the bolsheviks who set the precedent for the modern totalitarian leaders. Hitler and Mussolini were diligent students of bolshevik tactics, and now that these pretenders have been destroyed, we find, in state after state of Europe, the very shoes they walked in are being filled by agents of the soviet power centred in Moscow.
The nazis, and the bolsheviks are alike in that they are guided by only one political principle in seizing power. That principle is that the end sought justifies any means. They have the one-party system with its special privileged role in public life. They give the secret police a paramount position in the state. They organize and affiliate with similar parties abroad, and employ these parties for their own global and strategic purposes to fight democratic governments everywhere.
They assist their fellow travellers with public funds, and they give them the protection of their own diplomatic services. They direct them to attain their ends by sabotage and espionage. They employ the same technique in imprisoning political opponents and putting them to death by administrative decree; they have the same ideas about concentration camps, and the same primitive instincts that led them to inflict punishment on the families of their political exiles. They have the same methods of propaganda.
We have had in this country a partial expose of Moscow-directed espionage activities in our own public service. I did not agree with all of the government's methods, but I refrained from public criticism on the theory that the devil must be fought with fire. My only regret now is that the government did not act sooner; that it did not act more effectively, and that it is not now following through.
What is happening on our labour front? That is the part of our economy in which we should have the most concern at the present time. We have all heard of the Pat Sullivan exposures with respect to the Canadian Seamen's Union. I turn to the May 31 issue of Liberty, in which a well-known Ottawa correspondent deals with this subject under the startling caption, "Could the Reds Cripple Canadian Industry?" The author says, among other things:
If the communist party could bring simultaneous pressure in the vital spots where its influence is great, it could cause industrial chaos in wide areas of Canada.
And he says that on the available evidence the communists could now play havoc in the coal mines and fisheries of Canada, in our logging camps, in lake and coastal shipping, in great electrical manufacturing companies, and possibly in the automobile industry as well.
He maintains that in every one of these individual industries there have already been communistic red strikes. He points to the Sydney coal mines, to the maritime fisheries, British Columbia and Ontario logging camps, the Montreal and Toronto fur industry, the Ontario electrical factories, the Windsor automobile plants and Pat Sullivan's Seamen's Union which I have already mentioned.
This is a startling report going out from the capital city of this country, and written by a responsible member of the press gallery. Either these statements are true, or they are not. If they are true, the government should do something to correct t'he situation. If they are true, as many believe they are, the government should be ashamed of its own indecision in so important a matter.
We know now how these communistic organizations work. Every youth movement, every practical organization to improve the economy and social status of individual workers -all these the communists use, or try to use, for purposes that are not Canadian.
We know how difficult it is for some workers to resist them. We are promised during this session legislation covering a labour relations code. If this parliament cannot provide machinery so that Canadian organized labour can protect itself against communist activities, there is something sadly lacking somewhere. This parliament should see to it that Canadian labour unions, and Canadian cooperatives are not used by Moscow agents to become the stalking horses of the Soviet Union's imperial designs.
We in Canada are now no longer isolated from world affairs. We are now on the main highway over which this issue is likely to be
27ie Budget-Mr. Bracken

fought, if it is fought. Let us then address ourselves to the problem of mopping up communistic activities in Canada. There are many governments of many countries today hanging in the balance. They do not know which way to move. If they give the democratic process a chance they fear the great democracies will not back them up. This is one of the great hours for decision in our history and in the world's history. Canada should be prepared to make its decision, and let the whole world know what its decision is.
All dictatorships are alike to us. I believe that the second world war could have been prevented if the nations of the British commonwealth and the United States had let the dictators know in time that if they continued their aggressive ways they would have a fight on their hands.
What is mainly needed now is to let the communists know, in a frank but nevertheless friendly way, that, so far as we are concerned, they are entitled to their own type of economy, as long as they desire it, but that we have no use for their underground activities in this country, and that we propose to send their agents back home wherever we can root them out.
Let me now summarize briefly what I said in the earlier part of my remarks. With respect to the budget, it is dishonest in so far as it claims a real surplus. It has taken money secured from the sale of capital assets and counted it as current revenue, in order to say that it had a balanced budget. The surplus is said to be greater than any in Canadian history, greater than all surpluses put together. It well might be, because no other government in Canada had the assets arising from the expenditure of 810,000 million of the money of the Canadian taxpayers to sell, and then to apply the proceeds to the current revenues of the country.
The budget is also unsound in so far as it continues regressive taxation at its present height, thus levying an undue tax burden upon the poor. And it is misleading in so far as it leaves the impression that all is well in Canada. The government's policies are making us sell on credit at low prices in markets where much of the debt will not be repaid, and denying us the right to sell in a market where we can get higher prices in cash which we must have if we are not to run the risk of bankruptcy.
In regard to the government's motion asking us to approve a budget 300 per cent higher the third year after the war is over than in any previous peacetime budget, and giving us reductions of only seven per cent in the total tax for this year and twelve 
per cent for next year. On this matter our position is that the taxes in the budget are too high and that the tax reductions are too little.
With respect to the five criticisms in the amendments to which I have referred, the truth is simply and clearly stated in each of them. There has been no reduction in the regressive taxes, in the indirect, hidden taxes. There has been no stimulation of the development of our great primary industries of agriculture and mining upon which our internal and external problems so largely depend for solution. There has been no resumption of the dominion-provincial conference, which the government says it must have before it can carry out its own policies. Yet it neither carries out those policies nor calls a conference. It is afraid to meet the huge costs those policies involve and afraid to admit that it is afraid to face them. It is afraid to say it is going to add now or in the near future four or five or six hundred million dollars to the tax burden of this country. And so it does nothing. The budget does not increase the level of tax exemptions. It thereby imposes a tax upon people receiving incomes less than the amount necessary for a decent standard of living. Nor does it provide any relief for that half of the Canadian people who are below the level of income tax exemptions, and very little relief for large numbers of those above that level. The Minister of Finance spoke about a fifty-four per cent reduction in taxation at some of the lower income levels. But he did not emphasize that this fifty-four per cent reduction might mean only $6 a year in some cases, S10 a year in other cases, and $12 in others. So more than half the people of this country get' no relief at a time when their costs are going up and when added costs are put upon them through the action of the government in taking away its own subsidies.
In these circumstances, we in this party feel we have no choice but to support both the amendment and the subamendment to the budget motion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was just four weeks ago tonight that I had the honour of presenting to the house the government's financial proposals for the coming year. Since that time we have heard many speeches, most of them very good; and as usual in a budget debate they covered a wide variety of topics.
I do not propose to detain the house for more than a moment or two. In listening to those speeches-and I listened attentively to almost all of them-it seemed to me that

The Budget-Mr. Abbott
hon. gentlemen opposite were hard put to find any effective criticism of the budget proposals themselves. Such criticism as they made I think I shall be able to deal with when we are in the resolution stage, and rather than detain the house in the taking of the vote that is what I propose to do.
I cannot, however, allow the vote to be taken, without expressing my deep appreciation for the many generous personal references to myself which came from all sides of the house. Hon. gentlemen opposite confined their expressions of appreciation to the form rather than to the substance of what I had to say, but I attribute that fact to the natural and inevitable inclination of oppositions to show a singular lack of judgment with respect to proposals made by the government side of the house. Therefore I feel that I can take genuine satisfaction in the remarks they made with respect to myself personally as to the form. But with respect to hon. gentlemen on this side who praised the substance as well, I think they showed better judgment than hon. gentlemen opposite; and from what I have read in the press of the country, editorial comment and otherwise, I think their remarks reflect the judgment of the country as well.
However, I conclude these brief remarks by expressing my genuine appreciation of the very kind references which have been made from all sides of the house as to the manner of presentation, if not the substance.

This was denied by the then minister of finance, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley). We must accept his statement as an hon. member of this house, but we cannot accept-

Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
We cannot accept all that he said, in that the supposition was absurd. There are certain inescapable facts which I must bring before the house at the present time. The first question into which we must examine is this: Would the United States government have interfered-

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.
We must examine other actions of the government about that time, and it is germane to the subject to look at what the United States government did with regard to the extremely ticklish question of Palestine at the time. The United States government did interfere, and it interfered definitely and considerably, in that a statement was made last year at about the same time to the effect that, on the suggestion and request of the United States government, it was proposed that 100,000 Jews be admitted immediately into Palestine.
At that time the question of Palestine was one of the most ticklish in the entire international sphere. Therefore it is obvious that if the United States government would have interfered in that, they would have interfered in other matters. For the record I wish to quote two paragraphs from Keesing at page 8198:
In London, where President Truman's message caused much embarrassment and irritation, a government spokesman stated that on receiving the text of the message Mr. Attlee had immediately sent a request to the President to delay the issue of the statement until Mr. Bevin could be consulted and a further telegram sent to Washington explaining the British point of view, but that President Truman had replied that he was unable to comply with Mr. Attlee's request.
"The British government," said the spokesman, "has been working hard to bring the Jews and Arabs together. It is not correct that the discussions have been broken off. Consultations with the Jews are actually in progress at this moment. It is, in the British government's view, most unfortunate that a statement of this kind should have been made. It may well jeopardize the settlement of this difficult problem."
That is significant, because the statement of the President had been given to the British government before it was published. The British government protested that it should not be made, and the LTnited States government. went ahead and published the statement. The significant thing there is that the machinery used by Washington was to inform the

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
British government secretly of what it proposed to do before it did it. I wish to quote one more paragraph from the same authority, at page 8198:
It was felt in London and openly admitted in America that President Truman's message had been prompted by purely internal political considerations in view- of the forthcoming elections in New York state, with its important Jewish vote, and to anticipate a statement on the Palestine question by Governor Dewey on behalf of the Republican party.
I bring that up because it is important, for it shows that the United States government were prepared-that is the history of it-to interfere, and they were prepared to and, in fact, did interfere for political purposes, in the internal affairs of other states.
The second question that we must examine is this: Could the United States government have made the suggested proposition concerning parity? It is obviously impossible that the United States government could have made it now- with a hostile senate, a Republican controlled house and Republican controlled senate. But at that time the Democratic party was in control of both the senate and the house, and with an election year coming up, it is quite simple to understand that the administration could have put pressure on the members of its own party in both the house and the senate to assist this legislation, on a quid pro quo basis.
I wish to mention some of the statements made by Democratic members of the United States senate with regard to the British loan. These were made prior to the beginning of July. The first quotation I wish to use is from a radio speech by Senator Johnson of Colorado, on February 16, 1946:
The British loan is not to provide relief for starving people. It is to provide relief for a decadent empire. My slogan is: Billions for the relief of starving children but not one cent of American taxpayers' money for the relief of empires.
That is a Democratic senator. The next authority I have is Senator Wheeler, who was at that time chairman of the interstate commerce committee, one of the senior committees in the whole United States senate. He had this to say in a radio speech on February 16, 1946:
If we have $4 billion more to give away, let us turn our attention to the United States, where we have some very difficult problems. We have millions of veterans coming back. They are going to make large demands upon the country. We have slums all over the United States where the money could be used profitably for the public good.
That is an important Democratic senator.

speechtext:
He did, eventually. I now quote Senator McFarland of Arizona. I have the quotations here, and I shall be pleased to give them to Hansard, with the date and page of the Congressional Record. Senator McFarland had this to say, at page 4586 of the Congressional Record:
What I do want to address myself to is the proposition that our government should not enter into an agreement for a tremendous loan to a foreign power except on a sound business basis, w-hich cannot be done without first having reached some agreement and understanding with that power regarding an existing unpaid obligation. What I am contending for is simply plain common-sense business principles.
Then I quote Senator Richard B. Russell. And I may say that all these are Democratic senators and supporters of the administration. Senator Russell of Georgia had this to say, at page 4591 of the Congressional Record:
I referred, Mr. President, to the fact that future generations of Americans would be paying for the more than $40 billion of lend-lease supplied to our allies in this war. The same future generations, yet unborn, will be contributing taxes to defray the $4 billion British loan which is proposed by the pending joint resolution.
I think it is interesting to note that Senator Russell was one of those who changed their opinions and supported the resolution. Then w-e have Senator Johnston of South Carolina, who says this, at page 4333 of the Congressional Record:
I cannot even call this proposal a loan. It is, instead, the most munificent gift in history, and from the most heavily indebted nation in the world to a nation that will continue to be, as she always has been, unappreciative, unreliable, and totally without conscience in dealing with us.
That was a Democratic senator, a supporter of the administration. Then w-e come to Senator Allen J. Ellender of Louisiana, and his statement has a great deal of charm in it, which I am sure the house will appreciate. It is found at page 4187 of the Congressional Record:
So, in order to give the British the dominant position which they occupied in the past as was described by the distinguished senator from Utah, it will be necessary to keep on pouring money into London, just like pouring money into a rat hole, and expecting it to reach the rats. I simply cannot see it otherwise.
Then, of course, we get a statement from Bilbo. I w-ould not mention Bilbo because I do not think it is important, but he opposed
The Budget-Mr. Adamson

it, and I will just quote a line or two of what he said, as found at page 4160 of the Congressional Record:
Shall we grant this gift-loan to Britain? No, no, a thousand times no.
I have other quotations from the house of representatives which I shall not use, but there was a feeling which cannot be considered as anything but one of extreme hostility expressed by the Democratic party, with a Democratic President to a Democratic piece of legislation. These were only the people who spoke, but there were many others who opposed it. When a joint resolution was introduced into the senate, after all these condemnatory statements, the committee on banking and currency submitted the following report, and the date here is important. This is an extract from the Congressional Record, July 8, 1946, pages 8401-2, which was the beginning of the debate. Here is the Democratic party committee supporting the British loan, and it does so in these words:
The committee on banking and currency, to whom was referred the joint resolution (S. J. Res. 138) to implement further the purposes of the Bretton Woods Agreements Act by authorizing the Secretary of the Treasury to carry out an agreement with the United Kingdom, and for other purposes, having considered the same, report favourably thereon without amendment and recommend that the joint resolution do pass.
On the 4th of July we get condemnation from the Democratic party themselves, entirely outside the Republican party, and bitter denunciation of the bill. On July 8 we get a unanimous resolution from the Democratic committee on banking and currency, recommending that the loan do pass. What caused the change of policy?
Then we come to the next point we must observe. Was it to the advantage of Canada for the United States to pass the loan? We have just had' it pointed out tonight that we lent to the United Kingdom four times as much per capita as did the United States. Had the loan not passed, we in Canada and our entire economy would have been in serious jeopardy. We are in difficulty now. We do not see our way clear. We are in great fiscal difficulties with regard to exchange. But had this three and three quarter millions of hard currency not been available, nothing we could have done would have supported the United Kingdom or allowed the United Kingdom to have even a slim chance of recovery. I do not have to say to you, Mr. Speaker, or to the house, that unless we do have recovery in the United Kingdom, this country and1, in fact, the world will suffer a serious dislocation not only of trade, but of all peaceful commerce throughout the entire world. I say that with regard to the United Kingdom.

The next question we must ask ourselves is this: Was it to the advantage of the United States to have the Canadian dollar at par? I think the answer must again be yes.
