speechtext:
All right; I am merely making my statement, and I shall leave it to the house to decide.
Let us consider our trade with South America, one part of the world in which we were in competition with the United States. We look at United States exports to Latin America for the year 1946, based on the third quarter of United States trade, and which reached the large sum of 82 billion in exports and .81,777 million in imports. With Canada the United States exports were $1,555 million and the imports were S940 million. Trade with Asia, which was largely on a credit basis, was valued at 81,250 million, with imports valued at 8860 million. With England the exports are valued at 8740 million and the imports at $150 million.
That trade with South America and the Canadian trade with South America had increased in many instances as much as thirty-times over the pre-war figures. That was the point where Canadian trade was definitely in competition ' with United States trade, and the advantage that the dollar at a discount gave us was obviously of considerable value.
I have mentioned dates. The OP A lapsed on June 30; parity on July 6; the joint resolution was introduced on July 8 and passed on July 13-passed despite all adverse criticism, and with the united endorsation of the democratic committee on banking and commerce.
We are now asked to look at the government's case. First of all, I want to mention

The Budget-Mr. Adamson
one or two things parity has done to Canada. This very day we see the stringent restrictions on ownership of United States currency, scaled down to S10. The drain on United States currency in Canada must obviously be terrific, or the government would not have taken this emergency step. When 1 spoke on May 14 I suggested that there were three possibilities. They could reimpose restrictions; they could put up a tariff; they could devaluate. There was no other way, once this step had been taken, of preventing the drain on our currency.
The first step has already been taken; restrictions are being reimposed. The parity move has cost the country untold hundreds of millions of dollars. The first cost was the loss of S160 million in exchange. Equities in the stock market have decreased in the order of S200 million. Risk capital has all but dried up, and the production of vitally needed monetary gold is seriously restricted.
Those are the results. Why was this move made? We are asked by the government to believe that the move was made to protect the Canadian dollar against the inflation they suspected in the United States. If you have a suspected currency and you are worried about its worth, in order to protect your own currency do you tie your currency to the one that is suspected? I think that is most extraordinary. It is the same as the case of a man who, we believe, has smallpox. We are not sure, but we think that is the ailment from which he suffers. What we are going to do is that we are going to handcuff ourselves to him, get into bed with him, eat with his knife and fork and clean our teeth with his tooth brush. Is that the way to isolate ourselves from a contagious disease? Is tving our dollar to the United States dollar likely to isolate our Canadian dollar against the contagion of expected inflation? Could there not be some other reason?
The other reason advocated by the finance department was this, that we were frightened of the impact of panic United States money on the Canadian economy. We were frightened of loose United States funds coming into Canada putting up our price structure. There was one very simple way to overcome that. That was adopted, namely the procedure of putting on export embargoes in respect of certain foodstuffs. It was done at Windsor and at other border points where Americans came over and bought Canadian foodstuffs. There was a serious meat shortage at the time, and they were restricted in the amount
of meat and other foodstuffs they could export from Canada. It was a very simple thing which was done.
The second point is that theoretically they were frightened of United States panic dollars, United States currency coming into Canada and pushing up the price structure. That is inflation. But once you had secured your basic foodstuffs and your commodities, which was done, I suggest that a few hundred million dollars-if there were that much money of which the government was frightened- of United States funds coming into this country woidd be pretty useful to have in Canada at this time.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the reasons given by the government need further explanation. The results are becoming cumulatively more serious. The minister says those were the reasons for putting the dollar at parity. I accept his word; but I do say that the case for parity, as put forward by the government, needs more explanation than has been given thus far.

The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Special War Revenue Act and to provide:-
1.	That the tax in respect of transportation tickets or rights of transportation
(a)	be removed in respect of transportation by vessel or aircraft extending outside of the northern part of the western hemisphere, except in respect of any part of such transportation that is between any port or station in Canada or the United States and any other port or station in Canada or the United States; and
(b)	be extended to apply in respect of all transportation by vessel wholly within the northern part of the western hemisphere;
and that the second proviso to subsection 1 of section 32, under which section the tax is imposed, be repealed.
Will the minister give us an explanation of this change?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The purpose of the proposed amendment to the transportation tax is to bring the competitive position of Canadian companies into line with that of United States companies. Generally speaking, the amendment will exempt foreign travel under tickets purchased in Canada. The chief effect of the change, from the point of view of the Canadian tax, is to exempt transatlantic and transpacific air travel. Previously, air tickets from Canada to the United Kingdom have

Special War Revenue Act
been subject to tax. In future, no tax will apply on direct travel from a point in Canada to points in the United Kingdom. The tax will still be payable on tickets purchased in Canada for travel in and over the United States, just as tickets purchased in the United .States for travel to points in Canada will be taxable.
This is the only place that I can see where I can bring up the question in regard to the luxury tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid it would not be relevant to discuss luxury taxes under this resolution relating to the transportation tax.
This is the Special War Revenue Act, is it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, but this is a resolution on which will be founded a specific amendment to the war revenue act. The hon. member may have an opportunity to discuss the luxury tax on the second reading of the bill to amend the Special War Revenue Act, but under the rules of the house he cannot do so in connection with this resolution.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Under standing order 58 (2), all discussions in committee must be strictly relevant to the clause under consideration. At present we are considering clause 1, that the Special War Revenue Act be amended as indicated. It deals wholly with transportation, and I would ask hon. members to confine their remarks to the clause.
Then I take it that it will be all right to bring the matter up on the second reading of the bill to amend the Special War Revenue Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend will be perfectly free to say anything about the luxury tax when I move the second reading of the bill to amend the Special War Revenue Act.

Last year, during the budget debate, I brought up the question of taxation on air transportation to remote areas in Canada, and I have taken up the matter with the minister on several occasions. This is a very unfair tax on workmen working in the bush and mining districts, in that they have to pay fifteen per cent on air travel where there are no other means of communication. Take the district of Pickle Crow. The fare is $35 and the tax is approximately $6. For the same distance by rail, the tax would be seventy cents. I think it is very unfair that men working in remote areas should be called upon to pay a tax which, under normal conditions, if railways or bus lines were available, would amount to seventy cents, as against $6. I would ask the minister to consider the removal of this unjust imposition. This tax alone makes it difficult for mines operating in the Yellowknife, where the fare is $200 and there is a $30 tax, to get men into the area so that they can earn their living. It is time the tax was removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I gave consideration to the point which my hon. friend raised, as he said, and decided that I could not recommend this year the complete exemption of this transportation tax for that type of travel, but I am advised that, under the act as it stands, by a ruling of the Department of National Revenue, unscheduled trips pay only one cent per passenger mile, which is very much less, I am told, than the fifteen per cent tax.

What is meant by
unscheduled trips?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Where there is no regular route with a regular tariff, I am advised.
And no time table.

In those mining districts such as Red Lake, Pickle Crow, Yellowknife and San Antonio these are scheduled trips, and therefore these men going in there to earn their living must pay a fifteen per cent tax on air transportation, which is many times what they would pay on ordinary transportation, and it makes it very hard to get men to work in those areas.

I might add to what the hon. member has said. It was my privilege a year ago last winter to go into Red Lake on several occasions. At that time the Ontario government was trying to lay out the road to Red Lake, and it was difficult for them to get people into that district, difficult because once they get in there, it is hard for them to get out again owing to cost of transportation. They had to fly in and out. Now the Ontario government is building a highway in there which will make it a little easier. There is a community that,	once	they	can	get	housesbuilt, will be a	city	of fifteen	or	twentythousand in a short time. In fact, if they had houses today Red Lake would be a city of 20,000 people. It is difficult to get labour there to develop these mines, which would bring extra revenue to the country' and extra income tax. We should develop our gold resources, but people simply cannot afford to go in and out as they would like, and have their families, because	there	are	no	accommodations there	for	them	to	take their
families in. In such cases some special consideration should be given them.
Special War Revenue Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The point has been discussed with me and the officials of the department, and a number of hon. members who are familiar with conditions in the mining districts have also brought it up. After very careful consideration, I came to the conclusion that this year I could not exempt that particular class of travel within Canada from the fifteen per cent tax which applies to all air travel, with the exception of unscheduled trips where the special rate applies.

The committee is entitled to know the minister's reasons. He has the same opinion as he has held for some time, and I should like to know why, where there is no alternative means of mechanical transportation, this tax must apply. The hardships in these various regions, as has been pointed out, are rigorous, and everything should be done to encourage the development of these outlying territories, which are so rich in natural resources. Will the minister tell the committee his reasons? May I ask, further, where one can find the law that exempts unscheduled flights from the fifteen per cent tax?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are a variety of reasons. For one thing, it is difficult to confine the areas to which it applies.
An hon.	MEMBER:	Administrative
reasons?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, and they are important. Moreover, it is difficult to segregate luxury travel. Hunters, trappers, tourists want to go in and see these areas, and so on. On balance, I came to the conclusion that I was not justified in exempting this particular class at this time. The reasons may be good or they may be insufficient, hut there were a number of reasons.
Where does one find the law that exempts non-scheduled flights from the tax; or is it a departmental ruling?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am not familiar with
the details because it is not my own department, but I am advised that the particular reason is this. These are done on charter at a named rate and not in accordance with the recognized tariff, and the department ruled that the rate which would be established by the air transportation company, with one cent per passenger mile added, would be roughly comparable with the tax of fifteen per cent imposed on the regular scheduled tariff.

But the minister just
said it would not. The minister said that the tax on these unscheduled flights was small and did not compare with the fifteen

per cent tax, and now he tells us, on the advice of his assistants, that it is comparable. May I suggest to him that the people who use these non-scheduled flights are more likely to be in the luxury class to which he referred and which we should also encourage, although not at the cost of other less fortunate people. Hunters and fishermen are the ones who will get the non-scheduled planes more than the ordinary miners who go up to these out-of-the-way posts and develop our country. A group of these men do not hire a plane; they use the scheduled service and are subjected to a fifteen per cent tax. In other words, if there is any discrimination here at all, it is discrimination against the worker and in favour of the man who can afford to pay the tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed that there
is one added reason for the differentiation in connection with the unscheduled trips, namely, that in a good many cases the plane will carry a good deal of freight and equipment in addition to passengers. That is taken into account in fixing the one cent rate with respect to passengers.

Will the minister say
whether the tax is paid in full and a rebate given, or whether the tax is paid at the reduced rate when the transportation is arranged for? Is it necessary to arrange for each exceptional case, or is some organization set up which deals with cases of a specified character?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am informed that the
tax is collected at the time the payment is made for the flight.
I have been handed a pamphlet by someone. It is entitled "Ways and Means Resolutions, Resolutions of April 29, 1947; Income War Tax Act."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Over the page. We are
on the Special War Revenue Act legislation.

I am going to discuss the title of the copy I have in my hand. I want to know if Canada is still at war. I have asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare and others. Apparently we are still at war, and I should like to know with whom. No one has ever told me. I understood there was a proclamation at the beginning of the year stating that Canada was no longer at 'war. But I have sought to find out and I am told that we are still at war. If we are, I want to know whether we are at war with Russia, with the United States, or with whom?

With the government.

Special War Revenue Act
If this is the Income War Tax Act, I want to know with whom we are at war?

It is the Special War
Revenue Act.

It is the same thing. These people are talking about transportation into remote areas. I should like to get to my home once in a while, and that is not so remotely situated. But I want to know if Canada is still at war and, if we are, with whom we are at war. If we are not still at war, when was it determined that we are not at war? I do not know whether that is a proper question for the Minister of Finance, but no one has ever been able to tell me; and I have sent notes across the house hoping that those who favour me would advise me. We are apparently still at war with someone, but I do not know with whom.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will do my best to set my hon. friend's mind at rest. As he will see when the bill which is to be founded on the resolutions is brought in, we are removing the word "war" from the title and it will be called the Excise Tax Act.

In view of the situation which the hon. member for York South and others have placed before the house, I should like to move, seconded by the hon. member for York South:
That the following words be added to paragraph (a) of resolution No. 1: "or areas not served by any other form of transportation than aircraft."

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It occurs to me that this would disturb the balance of ways and means and accordingly would not be in order. I must therefore rule that the amendment would be out of order.
Let us carry them all if ;hat is the idea.
Are these words complete and significant enough to describe what is meant, "extending outside of the northern part of the western hemisphere"? What does that embrace?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course my hon. friend appreciates that the language of the resolution is not, as a rule, as specific as the language of the statute which will be founded upon it. I am advised that in the bill which will be introduced there will be definitions which will clarify exactly what that means.

I want to say one thing about this Red Lake business. In these remote areas-and Red Lake is remote, being 100
miles away from a railway-you cannot get there in any other way than by air, and the rates are about twenty cents a mile. I think the return there to Kenora is $36. Men going into Red Lake have to pay four times as much per mile for transportation, and there is the hardship owing to this tax, which is $3 one way and $6 return. That is quite a considerable outlay on top of the $36 you have to pay for transportation for the round trip.
Mr. Chairman-
Eleven o'clock.

Just before eleven o'clock, I want to urge, whether the motion is in order or not-and you have ruled it out of order, Mr. Chairman, and we accept that decision- that the minister give some consideration to the suggestion which has been made. After all, the revenue which is collected is very small in this case, and the hardships which have been mentioned are, I think, generally felt by a great many labouring men who cannot afford to pay the extra amount. I want to urge upon the Minister of Finance that he give some consideration to the suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before moving that the committee rise, may I say that I will give consideration to the matter again before I bring in the bill. As I say, I do not want to hold out very much hope, but I will take into consideration the points which have been brought forward here and discuss the matter again with the officials of the department.. I will consider it again before bringing in the bill. I move that the committee rise and report progress, unless you want to report this resolution.
No.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Does the committee desire to carry clause 1?

No.
Progress reported.
